1) the Cpa protein of S. pyogenes is a smart covalent bond, 2) Cpa is a catch bond, 3) the thioester bond of Cpa is reversibly reactive at low forces, but irreversibly reactive under large forces, and 4) the folding state of the Cpa protein is the key determinant of its adhesion strategy.
the folding of a bacterial adhesin controls its covalent anchorage to host surfaces.
the Cpa adhesin is equipped with a smart covalent bond that enables it to colonize mucosal tissue surfaces under large mechanical perturbances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanical properties and molecular dynamics of Cpa, a protein involved in the colonization of mucosal tissues by S. pyogenes.
the molecular mechanisms underlying bacterial adhesion and colonization, and the role of protein unfolding in the regulation of adhesin reactivity.
the molecular mechanisms of bacterial adhesins, and their ability to colonize host tissues against mechanical forces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thioester switch allows the adhesion molecule Cpa to switch between a “hopping” mode and a “locked” mode, and that this switch is governed by the force applied to the molecule.
the folding state of Cpa modulates the reactivity of the thioester bond, allowing for a dynamic adhesion strategy that combines both mobility and stability.
the thioester bond of Cpa is a catch bond.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Cpa thioether bond can be considered a “smart covalently bonded” adhesin, that can switch its mode of action between reversible and irreversible binding depending on the force applied.

the protein folding state modulates the Cpa thioesters reactivity, which allows the adhesion of the pathogen under mechanical stress, while enabling the bacterium to move over surfaces and colonize tissues.
Cpa thioesters are smart covalent bonds, and that the smartness comes from the ability of the protein to switch from a non-covalent to covalent adhesion state upon mechanical perturbation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

protein folding can be used to control the adhesion properties of the cell surface, and that the folding state of the adhesin can be used to regulate the adhesion strategy, which is essential for the pathogen to successfully colonize mucosal sites.
protein folding can control the reactivity of a thioester bond, and thus the ability to anchor a cell in place.

the folding of a protein adhesin is a crucial determinant of its ability to colonize surfaces, which has implications for understanding bacterial pathogenicity and designing novel antimicrobial agents.
